content: The system described automatically assigns a classification (green, amber, or red) to a facility based on specific indicators. If more than 30% of the required information is missing, the tool assigns a grey score. It aggregates facility-specific data into a single national report, providing both the facility and the national program with a color-coded performance summary. Countries are encouraged to harmonize the collection and reporting of these indicators by validating data through quality assessments, strengthening routine patient monitoring systems, and avoiding the creation of parallel systems. For pediatric populations, monitoring includes both general and HIV-specific indicators. Age disaggregation in five-year intervals is critical, as interventions often depend on the child’s age. Key general child health monitoring includes growth assessments (weight, height, and mid-upper arm circumference), developmental evaluations (motor, sensory, cognitive, communication, behavioral, social, and adaptive skills), immunizations per country-specific schedules, and infant feeding practices in the context of HIV. According to WHO guidelines, mothers living with HIV who are on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and have suppressed viral loads can breastfeed their infants for up to two years, with exclusive breastfeeding recommended for the first six months. Pediatric HIV monitoring also includes additional indicators beyond the 80 priority HIV indicators. These include immunization coverage (especially the first dose of diphtheria-pertussis-tetanus vaccine), breastfeeding practices, nutritional status, and nurturing care interventions. Infants exposed to HIV may be identified early if their mothers receive services for preventing vertical transmission or later if identified outside the prevention cascade. Infants identified as exposed during pregnancy or postpartum are classified as high or low risk for HIV transmission based on maternal ART use and viral load suppression. High-risk infants receive extended postnatal prophylaxis, while low-risk infants receive a single antiretroviral for six weeks. If the risk of transmission persists during breastfeeding, prophylaxis may be extended beyond 12 weeks. Late-identified HIV-exposed infants, particularly those whose mothers are not on ART or virally suppressed, may receive presumptive treatment with triple antiretroviral therapy. If HIV infection is ruled out, postnatal prophylaxis is provided as for high-risk infants. If infection is confirmed, presumptive treatment transitions to first-line ART as per WHO guidelines. Key indicators for monitoring include postnatal prophylaxis coverage, co-trimoxazole coverage, timing and duration of vertical transmission, antenatal and postnatal care attendance, maternal HIV testing and re-testing, maternal ART coverage during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and maternal viral suppression. For children living with HIV, monitoring focuses on transitioning to optimized ART regimens, such as dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens for children over 20 kg and lopinavir/ritonavir (LPVr) or DTG for those under 20 kg. As DTG becomes more widely available, transitioning children previously on LPVr to pediatric DTG should also be monitored. Treatment monitoring follows the WHO-recommended viral load algorithm, and access to psychosocial support for adherence is essential. The guidelines also emphasize the importance of monitoring vertical transmission prevention services across multiple service delivery points and over extended periods. This includes tracking mothers and infants from primary prevention and sexual/reproductive health services to HIV diagnosis, ART initiation, safe delivery, optimized infant feeding, and early diagnosis and treatment of infected infants. Tools must capture patient care workflows across different facilities and link mother-baby pairs using unique identifiers (UIDs). Integration of HIV and maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) services is critical, with patient monitoring systems supporting early provision of prevention interventions and tracking outcomes. Updated indicators for vertical transmission monitoring focus on outcomes such as viral suppression and early infant diagnosis, alongside intermediate outcomes like ART coverage during pregnancy and breastfeeding and infant antiretroviral prophylaxis. Seven national priority indicators are linked to critical time points in the vertical transmission risk period, helping countries strengthen data collection tools and quality assurance mechanisms for both patient care and program management. For TB-HIV co-infection, updates include indicators for TB preventive treatment (TPT) initiation and completion, TB diagnostic testing using molecular tools, and TB burden among new ART patients. Key interventions include ART initiation, intensified TB case-finding, TPT, and infection control.
